conventions: stop entries mechanized as signal-bar-close then next-bar-open; every tunable constant is a parameter; long side only in pseudocode. Helpers: range(n) = high[n]-low[n]; body(n) = close[n]-open[n]; avgRange(N) = average of range over the N bars ending at bar 1; upperTail(n) = high[n]-max(open[n],close[n]); lowerTail(n) = min(open[n],close[n])-low[n]; overlap(a,b) = min(high[a],high[b]) - max(low[a],low[b]); tick = instrument minimum price move (structural constant); highest(x,N)[k] / lowest(x,N)[k] = extreme over N bars ending at bar k.

candidates.name: BullReversalBarMinimum
candidates.quote: the minimum that a bull reversal bar should have is either a close above its open (a bull body) or a close above its midpoint.
candidates.description: Primitive: bar 0 qualifies as a (minimal) bull reversal bar if it closes up OR its close sits above its own midpoint. A bear reversal bar does not need its high to exceed the prior bar's high, only to reverse something about the prior price action.
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (bar classification used as a signal-bar test)
notes: Deliberately loose ('minimum'); T05-02/03/04 layer on the stronger quality tests Brooks lists.

p128: a bear reversal bar 'does not have to have a high that is above the high of the prior bar, but it does need to reverse something about the price action of the prior bar or bars' -- kept as the minimum bar, not tightened.

candidates.name: ReversalBarOpenNearPriorCloseStrong
candidates.quote: An open near or below the close of the prior bar and a close above the open and above the prior bar's close.
candidates.description: Quality test for a strong bull reversal bar: it opens at or below the prior bar's close (no gap against the reversal) and closes above both its own open and the prior bar's close.
candidates.pseudocode: open[0] <= close[1] + nearTicks * tick && close[0] > open[0] && close[0] > close[1]
notes: 'Near' is not quantified by Brooks; nearTicks(0) reads it as at-or-below.

candidates.name: ReversalBarTailFraction
candidates.quote: A lower tail that is about one-third to one-half the height of the bar and a small or nonexistent upper tail.
candidates.description: Quality test for a strong bull reversal bar: its lower tail is a moderate fraction of the bar's range and its upper tail is small or absent.
candidates.pseudocode: lowerTail(0) >= tailMinFrac * range(0) && lowerTail(0) <= tailMaxFrac * range(0) && upperTail(0) <= smallTailFrac * range(0)

candidates.name: ReversalBarLowOverlapFraction
candidates.quote: Not much overlap with the prior bar or bars. ... If a reversal bar largely overlaps one or more of the prior bars or if the tail extends beyond the prior bars by only a couple of ticks, it might just be part of a trading range.
candidates.description: Quality/filter test: the reversal bar shares only a small fraction of its range with the prior bar. Used positively (as a quality test for a strong reversal bar) and negatively (inverted, to reject a reversal bar that is mostly overlap, i.e. just part of a trading range).
notes: Direction-agnostic overlap measure; the 'tail extends beyond by only a couple of ticks' variant is the same idea applied to just the tail rather than the whole bar.

candidates.name: ReversalBarStrengthByClosesBeyondPriorBars
candidates.quote: if there is a bull reversal bar and its close is above the close of the past eight bars and its high is above the high of the past five bars, this is usually stronger ... than a reversal bar that has a close above only the close of the prior bar.
candidates.description: Strength gauge for a bull reversal bar: its close exceeds the closes of the last N bars and its high exceeds the highs of the last M bars (the more bars it reverses, the stronger the signal).
candidates.pseudocode: close[0] > highest(close, closeLookback)[1] && high[0] > highest(high, highLookback)[1]
notes: Brooks's minimum bar is 'more than one bar' (i.e., closeLookback/highLookback as low as 2); the 8/5 figures are his concrete strong example, kept as the defaults since they are his only stated numbers.

candidates.name: Ema20
candidates.quote: a market that has been in a trading range day until it reverses up strongly to just above the moving average ... Bull flags just above the moving average where there are three or more large bars that mostly overlap are usually traps.
candidates.description: Primitive: the 20-bar exponential moving average of closes; 'above the EMA' = close[0] > ema[0].
notes: Chapter does not repeat the '20' figure explicitly (it says only 'the moving average'); 20 is the corpus-standard EMA length used elsewhere in this book.

candidates.name: CountertrendRequiresTrendLineBreakAndTest
candidates.quote: When considering a countertrend trade in a strong trend, you must wait for a trend line to be broken and then a strong reversal bar to form on the test of the extreme, or else the chances of a profitable trade are too small.
candidates.description: Context filter: block a countertrend (reversal) entry in a strong trend unless a trend line has already been broken and the market is now testing the old trend's extreme with a strong reversal bar.

complexity.reason: needs trend-line-break detection (pivots + line projection) and a 'test of the extreme' swing-pivot test before it can be coded

notes: Related but distinct from the corpus's CountertrendSignalBarSmallerThanTrendBodiesFilter (T07-44), which only compares body sizes; this one additionally requires the trend-line-break/test structure.

candidates.name: ExcessiveOverlapMidpointFilter
candidates.quote: whenever the midpoint of a bull reversal bar is above the low of the prior bar in a possible bull reversal (or if the midpoint of a bear reversal bar is below the high of the prior bar in a possible bear reversal), the overlap might be excessive.
candidates.description: Block a bull reversal entry when the reversal bar's midpoint sits above the prior bar's low (the book's stated overlap guideline), more important for a countertrend attempt than a with-trend pullback entry.

complexity.reason: single comparison of a computed midpoint to a prior bar's extreme

notes: Transcribed literally from the book; as printed, the comparison is satisfied by nearly any bull reversal bar that doesn't gap down below the prior bar's low, which sits oddly with 'excessive overlap'. Flagging for the authoring pass to sanity-check against the book's figures before use, and consider whether Brooks meant the midpoint versus the prior bar's HIGH instead.

candidates.name: DojiLargeRangeNoReversalFilter
candidates.quote: If the body is tiny so that the bar is a doji but the bar is large, it usually should not be used as a basis for a reversal trade. ... It is better to wait for a second signal.
candidates.description: Block a reversal entry when the signal bar is a large-range doji (a small body relative to a large range): treat it as a one-bar trading range rather than a reversal.

candidates.name: LargeOppositeTailWeakensReversalFilter
candidates.quote: If a bull reversal bar has a large tail at the top or a bear reversal bar has a large tail at the bottom, the countertrend traders lost conviction going into the close of the bar and the countertrend trade should be taken only if the body looks reasonably strong.
candidates.description: Block a bull reversal entry when the bar has a large upper tail, unless the body is still reasonably strong (an override, e.g. for a second-entry-style confirmation).

candidates.name: SmallReversalBarWeakSignalFilter
candidates.quote: If the reversal bar is much smaller than the prior several bars, especially if it has a small body, it lacks countertrend strength and is a riskier signal bar.
candidates.description: Block a reversal entry when the signal bar's range is much smaller than recent bars and its body is small, unless the body is strong relative to the small bar's own range.
notes: Brooks: 'if the bar has a strong body and is in the right context, the risk of the trade is small' -- the override half of the filter.

candidates.name: TrendingTradingRangeDayReversalContext
candidates.quote: Most reversal bars on the daily chart come from trending trading range days ... Whenever traders see a trending trading range day, they should be aware that it might have a strong reversal later in the day.
candidates.description: Context filter: on a trending trading range day, favor reversal-bar entries later in the session (a permissive rather than blocking filter). Day-type classification itself is deferred to Chapter 22.

complexity.reason: 'trending trading range day' classification is a design decision, not yet defined

candidates.name: AlwaysInFlipOnStrongReversal
candidates.quote: A single strong reversal that reverses many closes and lows, like bar 29, can flip the always-in direction.
candidates.description: Treat a very strong reversal bar (one whose close reverses the closes and lows/highs of many prior bars) as flipping the market's 'always-in' direction, downgrading the reliability of any still-open pullback setups (high 1/high 2, low 1/low 2) in the old direction.

complexity.reason: 'always-in direction' is a design decision per the mining brief's own example; this chapter gives one concrete trigger for flipping it

notes: Bar 29's worked example reverses the closes of the prior 13 bars and the lows of the prior 12; kept generic rather than hard-coding those two numbers.
Brooks then expects trapped with-trend traders to place limit orders that themselves fail (high 1/high 2 as sell setups) -- narrative, not separately mined as a distinct bar-level test.

candidates.name: SecondFailedBreakoutAttemptReversal
candidates.quote: Bar 23 was a reasonable breakout pullback signal bar, since the market just made two attempts to sell off and both failed (bar 11 and the bar before bar 23).
candidates.description: After two separate attempts to break below a swing low both fail (each followed by a close back above the low), buy above the bar that reverses back into the range following the second failed attempt.
candidates.pseudocode: exists two bars j < k, both prior to bar 0, each closing below lowest(low, swingLookback) as of its own time and each followed within a few bars by a close back above that low; close[0] > high[1] as the entry trigger
candidates.book_order_type: buy stop one tick above the reversal (pullback) bar

complexity.reason: needs swing-low detection and counting two separate failed breakout attempts across a variable window

candidates.name: DojiEntryBarBreakevenExit
candidates.quote: Whenever the bar after the signal bar is a small doji bar, the market lacks urgency for a reversal. If the bar is an inside bar, ... it is usually better to not take the trade unless the setup is otherwise especially strong. If the doji is the entry bar ..., you can try to get out at breakeven or with a one-tick loss.
candidates.description: If the bar immediately after entry (the entry bar) closes as a small doji inside bar, the reversal lacks urgency: exit near breakeven rather than holding for the full target.
candidates.pseudocode: ctx.MarketPosition() > 0 && ctx.BarsSinceEntry() == 1 && high[0] <= high[1] && low[0] >= low[1] && abs(body(0)) <= dojiBodyFrac * range(0) && ctx.OpenPositionProfit() <= breakevenBandDollars
candidates.book_order_type: exit at or near breakeven (market or limit) on the doji entry bar's close

complexity.reason: position-state read (BarsSinceEntry, OpenPositionProfit) combined with a bar-pattern test

candidates.name: WeakSignalWeakEntryScratchExit
candidates.quote: When the entry bar after a weak signal is also weak, it is better to try to get out around breakeven.
candidates.description: If the original signal bar was weak (small body relative to its range) and the entry bar that followed it is also weak, exit near breakeven rather than holding for the target.
candidates.pseudocode: ctx.MarketPosition() > 0 && ctx.BarsSinceEntry() == 1 && abs(body(1)) <= weakBodyFrac * range(1) && abs(body(0)) <= weakBodyFrac * range(0)

complexity.reason: position-state read (BarsSinceEntry) combined with two-bar arithmetic

candidates.name: BullFlagOverlapTrapFilter
candidates.quote: Bull flags just above the moving average where there are three or more large bars that mostly overlap are usually traps. The same is true for a bear flag just below the moving average where there are three or more large bear bars that largely overlap.
candidates.description: Block a with-trend long entered above a signal bar sitting just above the EMA when that signal bar and the two bars before it are large and mostly overlapping (a common bull-flag trap, mirrored below the EMA for bear flags).
candidates.pseudocode: !(close[0] > ema[0] && range(0) >= largeMultiple * avgRange(rangeLookback) && overlap(0, 1) >= trapOverlapFrac * range(1) && overlap(1, 2) >= trapOverlapFrac * range(2))

complexity.reason: EMA plus a multi-bar overlap test

notes: Brooks estimates about a 60 percent trap rate for this pattern (p122's similar flag example uses the same figure).

candidates.name: SellingPressureAccumulationFilter
candidates.quote: Between bars 10 and 15 there were several bars with strong bear bodies and this was a sign of selling pressure. The pressure is cumulative, and it eventually led to a sell-off.
candidates.description: Treat several bars with strong bear bodies over a lookback window as cumulative selling pressure that favors a with-trend short entry even without one dramatic signal bar (mirrored: strong bull bodies favor a long).
candidates.pseudocode: count over k in 1..N of (body(k) < 0 && abs(body(k)) >= strongBodyFrac * range(k)) >= K

rejected.quote: Also, do not enter on a 1 minute reversal bar since the majority of them fail and become with-trend setups.
rejected.reason: chart bar-interval (1-minute vs. any other) is a configuration setting, not a value decidable from OHLCV bar data

rejected.quote: in the final few seconds before the bar closes, the price collapses and the bar closes on its low
rejected.reason: needs tick-level/intrabar data, unavailable at the completed-bar level

rejected.quote: what appears to be a perfect reversal bar on a 5 minute candle chart might not look anything like a reversal bar on many other charts ... don't waste your time looking around at dozens of charts for one where there is a perfect reversal
rejected.reason: requires comparing against other chart timeframes/resolutions the engine does not have; also pure discretion ('understand what the market is doing')

rejected.quote: raising the stop to just below a doji entry bar is not a good choice because the odds are 50-50 it will get hit
rejected.reason: describes a discretionary stop-placement judgment with no stated bar-level threshold beyond what T05-15/T05-16 already capture

chapter_summary: Defines the reversal bar as a signal bar: the minimum bull/bear reversal bar test (close beyond open or midpoint), the stronger quality tests (near-open, tail fraction, low overlap, closes beyond multiple prior bars), and a long list of filters for when a reversal bar should NOT be trusted (excessive overlap, large-range doji, large opposite tail, too-small range, trend-line-break/test-of-extreme requirement for countertrend trades, bull/bear flag overlap traps near the EMA). Also produced two exit rules for a weak entry bar (doji or weak-bodied) after the signal, an 'always-in flip' context idea tied to an unusually strong reversal, a second-failed-breakout reversal pattern, and a cumulative strong-body pressure filter. Primitives BullReversalBarMinimum and Ema20 are defined here per the one-per-file rule; BullReversalBarMinimum's threshold (close>open or close>midpoint) is looser than chapter 7's BullReversalBar (T07-03, which requires both a strong close position AND a lower tail) -- the dedup pass should treat T05-01 as the base primitive and T05-02/T05-03/T05-04 as the add-on quality tests that make it closer to T07-03.
